subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Coordination Games and Focal Points
description: A short lesson to help you apply Coordination Games and Focal Points.

hook.text: You must meet a stranger in New York City with no way to communicate. Most people independently choose Grand Central.

buildup.text: Coordination games have multiple equilibria. Success requires choosing the same option as the other player without.

discovery.text: Schelling found people use focal points: culturally prominent choices that stand out.

twist.text: Focal points are culturally specific. A Japanese pair might pick Shibuya Crossing.

climax.text: In business, standards become focal points. QWERTY, USB, and metric units coordinate behavior by being the obvious.

punchline.text: Without words, we find each other through shared expectations.

quiz.question: What is a focal point in game theory?
options: The optimal mathematical solution to a game
A culturally prominent choice that players independently gravitate toward
The point where both players decide to stop playing

details.summary: Coordination games have multiple equilibria where players need to choose the same strategy but have no way to communicate. Focal points, identified by Thomas Schelling, are salient solutions that people naturally converge on through shared culture.
details.whyItMatters: Many real-world problems are coordination games: which side of the road to drive on, which technology standard to adopt, which meeting place to choose. Focal points explain how people solve these problems without explicit agreement.
takeaways: Coordination games have multiple equilibria requiring players to match choices
Focal points are culturally salient solutions people gravitate toward
Thomas Schelling demonstrated focal points with his New York experiment

faq.question: What is Schelling's New York experiment?
faq.answer: Schelling asked people where they would meet a stranger in New York City with no prior arrangement. Most said Grand Central Station at noon. The clock there served as a focal point because of its cultural salience and centrality.

faq.question: How do focal points relate to social conventions?
faq.answer: Social conventions like driving on the right, using English in international business, or meeting at round hours are all focal points that emerged from coordination needs. Once established, they persist because deviating is costly.
